title.text:
What data science is
and how to think in it

objects.text: What does a data scientist do, and what will you be able to do after 24 sessions?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 1 of 24  |  Module A: Think with data
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome, everyone, and well done for coming after a full day of work. Over twenty-four sessions you will learn how people turn data into decisions. You start in a spreadsheet, which you already know, and you finish with a tested model and a small app that a colleague can open.

Today is the map. We look at what a data scientist does, how a data project is organised, and which free tools we use. Then you open a notebook and run your first line of Python.

Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can name the four roles on a data team and the six phases of the CRISP-DM lifecycle, which is the industry reference for how a data project runs. You can tell artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and data science apart by what each one produces.

And you can count the records and variables of a table in Google Sheets and run your first cell in Google Colab. Today is the lightest session of the course, so enjoy it.

We have two hours. The first ten minutes set the question of the day. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures and ask questions. After a ten minute break you open the Lakeside Mart workbook in Google Sheets and then a Google Colab notebook, for a forty-five minute lab.

The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Data science. Using data, tools and careful thinking to answer a question and support a decision. It is a way of working that runs from question to decision.

Machine learning (ML). A computer finds a rule from examples. A person does not type the rule.

Dataset. A collection of data about one subject, arranged in tables. In Excel words: a workbook in which each tab is one table.

Model. A rule found from data that turns inputs into a prediction or an explanation.

Lifecycle (CRISP-DM). The phases a data project passes through. CRISP-DM is the industry reference: six phases, from business understanding to deployment.

title.text:
Data science turns a question
and data into a decision

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_7.70x4.80_f299f963.png
objects.alt: Data science turns a question and data into a decision

objects.text: Data science is a way of working: someone asks, data answers, and a person decides.

runs.text: Dataset: a workbook in which each tab is one table.
Model: a rule found from data. You fit your first model in Session 13.
A chart nobody uses has failed.

slides.notes:
So what is data science?

My answer is simple. It is a way of working that turns a question and some data into a decision. It starts with a decision that somebody has to make. Then you find the data, which means rows and columns, the same as in your spreadsheets. In Excel words, a dataset is a workbook where each tab is one table.

Then you apply a method. Mostly that is counting, charts and careful comparisons, and sometimes a model, which is a rule found from data. It ends with advice a manager can act on. Which of the four boxes do you think people forget most often?

title.text:
A business question worth asking
names the decision it feeds

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: A weak question

runs.text: Tell me about sales.
No decision attached.
No number to find.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: A strong question

runs.text: Which branch has the lowest median order value this quarter, so it gets next month's support visit?
It names the measure (median order value) and the decision (the support visit).
The Lakeside workbook has the data.

objects.text: Write the decision first, then the question.

slides.notes:
Every project starts with a question, and most weak projects start with a weak question. Tell me about sales is weak. It has no decision attached, no number to find, and no sign of when you are done. Which branch has the lowest median order value this quarter, so it gets next month's support visit, is strong.

It names what to measure, which is the median order value. It names the decision it feeds, which is the support visit. And it needs data you can actually get, which is the Lakeside workbook. So write the decision first, then the question. Think of one question from your own work.

Is it weak or strong?

title.text:
CRISP-DM, the industry reference,
splits a data project into six phases

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_cycle_11.90x4.25_451abd04.png
objects.alt: CRISP-DM, the industry reference, splits a data project into six phases

objects.text: CRISP-DM: Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining. A later phase can send you back.

slides.notes:
This circle is the lifecycle, and it has a real name that you will meet in job adverts and textbooks. It is called CRISP-DM, which stands for Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining. It was written down in the late 1990s and many teams still use it. It has six phases.

Business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment. Data sits in the middle because every phase touches it. The arrows go round, but you also go back. If evaluation shows a problem, you return to an earlier phase. Which phase do you expect to take the most time?

slides.notes:
Here is each phase with the plain question it answers, and where we do it in this course. Business understanding asks what decision we are helping with. Data understanding asks what each table and variable means. Data preparation is cleaning and joining. Modelling asks which rule fits the data.

Evaluation asks whether the result is good enough and fair. Deployment asks how other people use it. Many teams add a seventh step, monitoring, where you check later that it still works. The session numbers are the plan today and may shift a little. Which phase is the first one you would hand to a colleague?

title.text:
One Lakeside question
walks through all six phases

rows.text: Decide which branch gets next month's promotion budget.
The orders tab has 2,000 records. The branches tab has 8 records.
580 orders have a blank customer_id. They are walk-in shoppers, so keep them.
A pivot table of orders and total sales for each branch. A predictive model comes in Module D.
Jinja leads on the mean order, 71,914 UGX. One order of 1,935,520 UGX adds about 7,300 UGX to that mean, but Jinja still leads without it. Check the median and the count too.

slides.notes:
Let us walk one real question through the six phases. The question: which branch gets next month's promotion budget?

Data understanding: the orders tab has 2,000 records and branches has 8. Data preparation: 580 orders have a blank customer id. They are walk-in shoppers, so we keep them. Modelling: a pivot table is enough here. Evaluation matters most. Jinja leads on the mean order, about 71,914 shillings, but one single order of 1,935,520 shillings adds about 7,300 shillings to it.

Jinja still leads without that order, so we check the median and the count before we decide. And deployment is one page for the manager. Would you have caught that large order?

title.text:
Thinking in data means four habits, and
you practise each one in this course

objects.text: Before you touch a number, ask these four things.

objects.text: What does one record stand for?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.70.png

objects.text: Where did the data come from, and how many records are there?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.70.png

objects.text: Did I calculate this number, or did someone tell me?

slides.notes:
Beyond the lifecycle, here are four habits that mark someone who thinks in data. First, what decision is this for?

Second, what does one record stand for?

Is each row an order, a product on an order, or a customer?

Third, where did the data come from, and how many records are there?

A figure from twenty records means something different from a figure from twenty thousand. Fourth, did I calculate this number, or did someone tell me?

Session 2 teaches the second habit properly. Which of the four is hardest for you at work?

title.text: Four roles share the work on a data team

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_icons_11.90x4.25_49fae6d1.png
objects.alt: Four roles share the work on a data team

objects.text: One person often does several jobs. You practise the analyst and scientist jobs.

slides.notes:
Data work is a team sport, and four job titles come up again and again. The data engineer builds the pipelines that move data and keeps the databases running. The data analyst answers questions about the past with tables, charts and dashboards. The data scientist tests ideas and builds models that explain or predict.

And the machine learning engineer puts a model into a product and keeps it running. In a small organisation in Uganda, one person often does several of these jobs. In this course you practise the analyst and the data scientist jobs. Which of the four is closest to your job today?

title.text:
Artificial intelligence, machine learning,
deep learning and data science differ

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_nested_11.90x4.25_f851f772.png
objects.alt: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and data science differ

objects.text: Data science is the way of working, and often needs no machine learning.

slides.notes:
You hear three big words in the news. Artificial intelligence is the biggest circle. It means any software that does a task we would call smart, like a spam filter. Machine learning sits inside it. These programs find rules from examples, and the result is a model. Deep learning is a smaller circle inside machine learning.

It uses neural networks with many layers, and it powers speech recognition. Data science is different. It is a way of working from question to decision, and it uses machine learning only when that helps. Often a pivot table is enough. Which circle did you think data science was?

title.text:
A formula is a rule you write; a
model is a rule found from data

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.75.png

objects.text: Rule written by a person

runs.text: Revenue = quantity × price × (1 − discount).
It holds on all 6,590 order lines.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_robot_0.75.png

objects.text: Rule found from examples

runs.text: Nile Microfinance: 8,000 loans, 1,004 defaulted.
An algorithm finds which loan details go with default.

objects.text: A model is a rule found from data.

slides.notes:
Here is the difference between a formula and a model. On the left, a rule that a person wrote. Revenue of an order line is quantity times unit price times one minus the discount. We checked, and it holds on all 6,590 order lines in the workbook. On the right, a rule found from examples.

In the fictional Nile Microfinance file, 8,000 past loans are recorded and 1,004 of them defaulted. A learning algorithm looks at the loan details and finds which ones go with default. Nobody typed that rule. That is machine learning, and you fit your first model in Session 13 (regression) and build machine learning models from Session 14.

Can you think of a rule in your work that nobody could write by hand?

title.text:
Lakeside Mart is the real
data for the whole course

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_icons_11.90x4.25_7cac3d9c.png
objects.alt: Lakeside Mart is the real data for the whole course

objects.text: Fictional, generated data. A sample of a 30,229-order file.

slides.notes:
Now the data we use all course. Lakeside Mart is a fictional chain of eight mini-markets in Uganda. The workbook has 7 tabs: six data tabs and a READ ME. The orders tab has 2,000 records. Each record is one till order. The order lines tab has 6,590 records, one for each product on an order.

There are 8 branches and 150 products. The workbook is a sample of 2,000 orders from a full file of 30,229. Everything is generated, so no real person or company appears. In Session 2 we look at every tab closely. Which table would you open first?

title.text:
A chat assistant can state a
figure that nobody calculated

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: Unchecked

runs.text: You ask for the share of orders paid by Mobile money.
It answers with a clean percentage.
It predicts likely words and may not calculate.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: Checked

runs.text: One COUNTIF formula in Sheets gives it.
976 of 2,000 orders: 48.8 percent.
Write the source beside the figure.

objects.text: Recompute every number you did not calculate yourself.

slides.notes:
This habit will protect your reputation. You ask a chat assistant what share of orders is paid by mobile money. It answers with a clean percentage in a friendly tone. An assistant predicts likely words, so it can state a figure that nobody calculated. Nothing in its tone tells you which figures are real.

The check takes one formula in Sheets: count the orders paid by mobile money and divide by all orders. The answer is 976 out of 2,000, which is 48.8 percent. Write the source beside the figure. A free assistant is welcome as a helper in this course, but never as the source of a number.

Have you ever pasted a number you did not check?

slides.notes:
Here is the path for the whole course. Module A, today and the next three sessions, is thinking with data in Sheets, with no code. Module B teaches Python for data. Module C is analysing and explaining: SQL, charts, inference and regression. Module D is machine learning, where you build, test and judge models.

Sessions 8, 13, 19 and 24 have a project milestone, a practical piece of work that you show me and get feedback on. Nothing in this course is scored, and you keep everything you build.

Forty-eight hours is short, so we choose the working core of the field. Which module are you most looking forward to?

title.text: Colab is free, with limits to plan for

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_icons_11.90x4.25_06abbdf7.png
objects.alt: Colab is free, with limits to plan for

objects.text: My understanding at the time of writing. Check current limits.

slides.notes:
Colab is free, and free comes with limits. A free session ends after you stop working for a while, which is the idle time. A session also ends after a maximum length. Reports mention about twelve hours, but Google does not publish exact limits, and they can change.

So plan for it from day one. Save your notebooks in Google Drive or on GitHub, and run the cells again from the top when a session ends. That is my understanding at the time of writing, so check the current limits before you rely on a long run.

Where will you keep your notebooks?

title.text:
A notebook is made of cells: text
cells you read and code cells you run

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_notebook_11.90x4.25_7cf65094.png
objects.alt: A notebook is made of cells: text cells you read and code cells you run

objects.text: Python is the programming language. A cell is one box of code. Run it, read it, change it, save it.

slides.notes:
This is what a notebook looks like. It is a document made of cells. A text cell, marked one, holds instructions that you read. A code cell, marked two, holds Python, and you run it with the play button beside it. The output, marked three, appears under the cell.

In this picture the code stores a sentence in a name called message and then prints it, and the sentence appears. We ran this exact code to get that output. You can edit any cell, run it again, and see the output change. That is the whole loop.

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: A count of 2,001 where you expected 2,000
The range includes the header cell in row 1.
Start the range in row 2: A2:A2001.
You ran a cell before the cell that creates the name.
Run the cells from the top, one after the other.
A quote mark is missing at one end of the text.
Put the same quote mark at both ends: 'text'.
The setup cell has not run, or data.zip was not chosen.
Run the setup cell and choose data.zip.
Reconnect, run from the top, and save a copy to Drive.
